titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House

div.head: 395. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House
div.p: Secto 15096. Subject: Memorandum for the President.
Subject: My day in Ecuador, August 10.

2. Today I attended President Borja’s inauguration in Ecuador and sat through his two-and-a half hour inaugural address. His speech was a bigger bomb than the one that hit my motorcade in Bolivia, and Fidel Castro himself was sitting up there on the platform consulting his watch and muttering that it would never end.

3. During the day I had a series of interesting meetings. The Chilean Foreign Minister said their plebiscite was on track, but I told him we’d like to see it be truly fair, including fair access to TV for
the opposition. I told Columbia’s Pres. Barco how impressed all Americans are with his brave fight against the deadly drug trafficker-guerrilla alliance. And Portugal’s Pres. Soares told me he had met with Castro and was moderately optimistic that a settlement in Angola might be forthcoming.

4. I also had a good private meeting with Borja and lunch with his economic team. He and they seemed serious and well-intentioned, and I wished them the very best. The extreme leftist head of the Congress commissioned a mural for the hall where the inauguration was held. And the painter—another leftist who was Castro’s host there—included a Darth Vader-like figure with the letters “CIA” on his helmet. Borja apologized and noted he couldn’t control what Congress had done. And I told a press conference that the message of the mural was insulting to the US, but that if a bomb hadn’t driven us out of Bolivia, a mural wasn’t going to keep us away from this inauguration in Ecuador. A lot of Ecuadorians agree, and one Quito paper editorialized today that “What happened is damnable because it shows in both the artist and the commission-giver a skewed knowledge of history—product of a generalized anti-American prejudice.”

5. But while Borja talked sense privately, his inaugural address seemed to collect every bad idea of the last fifty years. (Maybe that’s why it was so long: That’s a lot of territory to cover.) He began with a very good section on the crucial importance of democracy, but went on to a strange pastiche of intellectual pretension, economic illiteracy, and an endless recitation of statistics. By the time he
finished, his popularity rating had probably dropped ten points.

6. One final point: Quito is smashingly beautiful. A city of hills and valleys 9,600 feet up in the Andes, it is clean, unmarred by visible poverty, and with enough of the old colonial heritage visible to remind you of Spain. Borja is a social democrat, and I left hoping he, like Mitterrand, will drop the ideology and do what works to help the people of that lovely land.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 22C, 1988 June–August, Memoranda for President Ronald Reagan. Secret; Immediate; Nodis; Eyes Only. Sent from the Delegation’s aircraft. Shultz travelled to Quito to meet with President-elect Borja, August 10.

In telegram 6140 from Quito, May 9, the Embassy reported the unofficial results of the May 8 presidential election with Borja winning by 190,000 votes. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880398–0684) In telegram 10567 from Quito, August 11, the Embassy sent an overview of Borja’s inaugural address, which “emphasized the theme ‘peace and unity’ but called upon the nation to make considerable sacrifice to pull Ecuador out of its ‘chaotic’ economic situation.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880705–0315)

See Document 396. In telegram 10530 from Quito, August 11, the Embassy reported on Shultz’s August 10 luncheon meeting with Borja’s economic team. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880704–0606))

Telegram Secto 15089 from Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation, August 10, transmitted the text of Shultz’s press statement. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880700–0278)
